scenario.gentle: A couple finally gets dinner together, but work notifications keep pulling one partner out of the conversation.
scenario.direct: The relationship moment is being interrupted by an external trigger with social permission attached to it.
scenario.competitive: The third guest at dinner keeps vibrating on the table.

whatToDo.gentle: Create a spoken boundary for the meal and put the device physically out of reach before the conversation starts.
whatToDo.direct: Use a pact that protects the room instead of trusting willpower against a live trigger.
whatToDo.competitive: Throw the intruder out before the first course.

whyItMatters.gentle: That does not create warmth by itself, but it gives warmth a place to arrive.
whyItMatters.direct: Structure protects the conditions of presence even though presence still has to be practiced.
whyItMatters.competitive: First clear the room, then be in it.

examples.title: The after-work debrief that keeps drifting

scenario.gentle: One partner says they want to hear about the other's day, but they keep half-scrolling while listening.
scenario.direct: The issue is not lack of stated care but chronic partial attention.
scenario.competitive: The ears stay seated while the eyes defect.

whatToDo.gentle: Choose one short no-scroll debrief ritual after work and keep it small enough to be repeatable.
whatToDo.direct: Protect one recurring window where the partner receives undivided attention instead of commentary plus drift.
whatToDo.competitive: Give the bond ten clean minutes instead of thirty torn ones.

whyItMatters.gentle: Repeated presence can rebuild trust faster than occasional grand gestures.
whyItMatters.direct: A defended ritual changes what the partner actually experiences, not just what is intended.
whyItMatters.competitive: Consistency starts paying down the fragment debt.

scenario.gentle: A tense conversation turns vulnerable, and one partner suddenly reaches for their phone or invents a small task.
scenario.direct: An internal trigger is driving the distraction pattern.
scenario.competitive: The hand grabs an exit when the feeling gets hot.

whatToDo.gentle: Name the discomfort and agree on a short pause or return time instead of disappearing into a vague distraction.
whatToDo.direct: Use the framework honestly by treating the urge to escape as an internal trigger rather than as a harmless habit.
whatToDo.competitive: Call the escape hatch by its real name and set a re-entry timer.

whyItMatters.gentle: That keeps avoidance from quietly teaching the relationship that hard feelings must be faced alone.
whyItMatters.direct: Repair becomes more possible when the escape is named and bounded.
whyItMatters.competitive: The room stops watching one person vanish through a side door.

examples.title: The date night that became logistics

scenario.gentle: A couple protects weekly time together, but the whole block gets consumed by errands, scheduling, and reactive cleanup.
scenario.direct: The calendar is working, but presence inside the block is leaking away.
scenario.competitive: The reservation survived; the evening did not.

whatToDo.gentle: Keep the protected time, then add one simple rule that separates logistics from connection for part of the evening.
whatToDo.direct: Treat scheduling as necessary but incomplete by protecting some portion of the block for actual attention.
whatToDo.competitive: Save part of the room from paperwork.

whyItMatters.gentle: That honors the chapter's limit that structure cannot replace intimacy but can defend it.
whyItMatters.direct: The couple stops confusing shared administration with shared presence.
whyItMatters.competitive: The room gets people back, not just calendars.

scenario.gentle: One partner keeps bringing laptop work into the last part of the night even though both say they miss each other.
scenario.direct: Work has become the default claimant on the relationship's closing hour.
scenario.competitive: The office keeps sleeping in the bed.

whatToDo.gentle: Create a clear evening cutoff pact and a backup plan for unfinished work earlier in the day.
whatToDo.direct: Use a spoken boundary so the relationship does not keep losing by default to spillover.
whatToDo.competitive: Evict the office before lights-out.

whyItMatters.gentle: That protects a recurring zone where closeness can actually happen.
whyItMatters.direct: Pacts matter because some relational boundaries hold better when they are explicit and pre-decided.
whyItMatters.competitive: A lock on the office door saves the bedroom from becoming annexed.

examples.title: The repair after the glance away

scenario.gentle: A partner notices the familiar distracted glance and names feeling unseen instead of letting the moment harden into resentment.
scenario.direct: The relationship has a chance to repair the pattern before it becomes atmosphere.
scenario.competitive: The fracture is caught while it is still a crack.

whatToDo.gentle: Respond with attention and repair instead of defending the habit as trivial or inevitable.
whatToDo.direct: Treat the moment as relational data and reconnect before the pattern gets another repetition.
whatToDo.competitive: Face the crack before it learns masonry.

whyItMatters.gentle: Quick repair can keep chronic distraction from becoming the background climate of the bond.
whyItMatters.direct: The chapter ends with presence as something practiced and renewed, not assumed.
whyItMatters.competitive: The room stays livable because the leak gets patched while it is small.

coreSkill.gentle: Protect one recurring relationship moment from the distraction pattern that most often steals it.
coreSkill.direct: Use the framework to defend intimacy from internal escape and external interruption.
coreSkill.competitive: Take one hour back for the bond and then show up inside it.

plan.gentle: If a close relationship keeps receiving my leftover energy at night, then I will protect one small evening window before everything else spills into it.
plan.direct: If the bond keeps losing the end of the day by default, then I will create a defended relationship block and treat it as traction.
plan.competitive: If the night keeps being mugged, then I post a guard at the door.

plan.gentle: If work keeps following me into relationship time, then I will create a clearer cutoff and a better earlier containment plan.
plan.direct: If professional spillover keeps fragmenting intimacy, then I will use a pact rather than a nightly promise to 'be better.'
plan.competitive: If the office keeps sneaking home, then I change the locks.

plan.gentle: If I notice myself escaping a hard feeling through distraction, then I will name the discomfort and return on purpose instead of vanishing into it.
plan.direct: If an internal trigger starts pulling me out of connection, then I will treat it as part of the framework and repair quickly.
plan.competitive: If the exit hatch opens, then I label it and come back through the front door.

twentyFourHourChallenge.gentle: Within the next day, protect one relationship moment from its usual distraction pattern and notice what changes when presence has room.
twentyFourHourChallenge.direct: Run a 24-hour intimacy-defense move around one recurring trigger.
twentyFourHourChallenge.competitive: Reclaim one hour before tomorrow closes.

weeklyPractice.gentle: At week's end, review which moments of closeness received defended presence and which still lived on leftovers.
weeklyPractice.direct: Compare your stated relational importance to the attention your partner actually experienced.
weeklyPractice.competitive: Audit who got your fragments and who got your face.
